item.title: Fiji must stay prepared – Pio
item.description: FIJI cannot always predict the challenges that may confront it but it could prepare itself to respond with greater coordination, says Home Affairs Minister Pio Tikoduadua. While commending security agencies involved in the multi-agency program, Exercise Bougainville, Mr Tikoduadua said Fiji’s national security extended beyond its shores.
item.content:encoded:
FIJI cannot always predict the challenges that may confront it but it could prepare itself to respond with greater coordination, says Home Affairs Minister Pio Tikoduadua.

While commending security agencies involved in the multi-agency program, Exercise Bougainville, Mr Tikoduadua said Fiji’s national security extended beyond its shores.

“On Tuesday, 25th August, I had the opportunity to return to witness the culmination of the exercise as it moved into its final Deployable Condition (DepCon), based on a simulated maritime incursion at Serenity Island,” he said.

“The exercise scenario involved a group taking control of the island and using it as a point for transportation of illicit drugs and weapons.

“This triggered our defence and policing forces to deploy and test their interoperability and response across governance, capacity and capability.”

He said exercises such as Bougainville allowed security agencies to train together, test the systems and capabilities, and strengthen the coordination that would be essential when responding to a real crisis.

“For me, seeing this exercise unfold was also a reminder that our national security responsibilities extend well beyond our shores.

“Our maritime space connects our islands, supports our communities and economy, and is an important part of what we must be prepared to protect.

“Exercise Bougainville 2026 is ultimately an investment in our people and in our preparedness.”

item.content:encoded:
THE proposed Fiji-Australia Veitacini Treaty is set to strengthen infrastructure at the Queen Elizabeth Barracks while creating greater support for veterans, including improved access to healthcare and dedicated services.

Minister for Defence and Veteran Affairs Pio Tikoduadua told the Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs and Defence on Thursday that infrastructure development was an important component of the treaty’s 10-year plan.

He said the Republic of Fiji Military Forces (RFMF) had recently taken ownership of a fully equipped gym at Queen Elizabeth Barracks, aimed at improving the health and wellbeing of service personnel.

Mr Tikoduadua said a $2.7million armoury project at the barracks was 72 per cent complete.

He said a further $2.2m renovation of the RFMF Commander’s office was 38 per cent complete and expected to be finished by November this year.

On veterans, he said Fiji had requested support under the treaty to improve healthcare access and explore dedicated funding for veterans’ programmes and services.

item.title: Suliana wears her heritage with pride
item.description: FMF Hibiscus Festival iTaukei Night winner Suliana Latianara turned her victory into a celebration of heritage, carrying the stories of two ancestral homes onto the stage through her traditional attire. For the Nacamaki, Koro lass who is sponsored by Fiji Rugby, the win was made even more meaningful by the story woven into the design.
item.content:encoded:
FMF Hibiscus Festival iTaukei Night winner Suliana Latianara turned her victory into a celebration of heritage, carrying the stories of two ancestral homes onto the stage through her traditional attire.

For the Nacamaki, Koro lass who is sponsored by Fiji Rugby, the win was made even more meaningful by the story woven into the design.

“This traditional attire is more than a costume; it is a story of identity, ancestry and belonging,” she told the crowd.

The front design represented her koro ni vasu (maternal links), Baravi Navakasiga in Bua, featuring natural tones, woven details, floral adornments and traditional patterns reflecting her people and their connection to the land.

The back portrayed her paternal roots in Nacamaki, Koro, Lomaiviti.

“I am a young woman carrying two homes, two stories and generations of heritage with pride.”

item.title: Leptospirosis claims youngest life
item.description: A 14-YEAR-OLD from Bagata, Savusavu, was the youngest person to die from leptospirosis at Labasa Hospital. The child was among the 16 deaths recorded in the hospital’s Intensive Care Unit over a 12-month period.
item.content:encoded:
A 14-YEAR-OLD from Bagata, Savusavu, was the youngest person to die from leptospirosis at Labasa Hospital.

The child was among the 16 deaths recorded in the hospital’s Intensive Care Unit over a 12-month period.

The figures were highlighted by Miss Labasa Divisional Hospital Isabella Raidriwa, one of seven contestants vying for the Vodafone Miss Friendly North title.

She said the hospital’s laboratory department recorded nine cases of typhoid fever, 640 cases of dengue fever and 226 cases of influenza-like viral infections during the reporting period.

“The ICU recorded 16 deaths between March 2025 and March 2026, with the youngest being a 14-year-old who died from leptospirosis,” she said.

“There’s a need of practising good hygiene, including covering the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing and washing hands before eating or preparing food and after using the toilet.”

She also encouraged young farmers to wear protective gear, including gloves and gumboots, when working with livestock or on farms.

“If you are experiencing these flu-like symptoms, please boost your immunity by eating healthy food and staying hydrated.”

She said communities also needed to work together in protecting their environment by clearing possible mosquito breeding sites.

item.title: Court rejects hearsay challenge
item.description: A COMPANY document containing details of directors and secretaries will be admitted into evidence in the trial of former deputy prime minister Professor Biman Prasad. Magistrate Yogesh Prasad dismissed the defence’s hearsay objection, which argued that the document should not be admitted because its maker was not available for cross-examination.
item.content:encoded:
A COMPANY document containing details of directors and secretaries will be admitted into evidence in the trial of former deputy prime minister Professor Biman Prasad.

Magistrate Yogesh Prasad dismissed the defence’s hearsay objection, which argued that the document should not be admitted because its maker was not available for cross-examination.

Defence submitted that the document raised issues concerning its credibility, reliability, and truthfulness.

The prosecution argued the document was a statutory form lodged with the Registrar of Companies and formed part of the public records maintained under companies legislation.

In his ruling, Magistrate Prasad noted that hearsay evidence is generally inadmissible when it is relied on to prove the truth of its contents, but recognised exceptions exist.

He found the document fell within an exception to the hearsay rule, noting it was lodged by a company representative and accepted into the register by the Registrar after statutory requirements were met.

The defence objection was dismissed, and the trial resumes on Monday at 10am.

item.title: Dry spell hits North farmers
item.description: THE prolonged dry spell has had a huge impact on farmers in the North, with the dry conditions affecting crop production. While raising his concerns about food security, the principal agriculture officer Northern Surendra Prasad said farmers needed to find ways to continue producing crops despite the current weather conditions.
item.content:encoded:
THE prolonged dry spell has had a huge impact on farmers in the North, with the dry conditions affecting crop production.

While raising his concerns about food security, the principal agriculture officer Northern Surendra Prasad said farmers needed to find ways to continue producing crops despite the current weather conditions.

“We are experiencing prolonged dry weather, which means drought. Our Fiji Met has predicted this drought will continue until January,” he said.

Mr Prasad said farmers needed to consider what changes could be made to maintain food production during the dry period.

“Climate change is now a reality and farmers needed to adjust to changing weather conditions.”

He said farmers were problem-solvers who had to find ways to grow crops despite unpredictable weather.

“The prolonged dry conditions could affect the amount of produce available for families and markets and also affect farmers who depend on crops for income.”

He urged farmers to seek advice from agriculture officers on suitable farming methods during the dry spell.

“Agriculture teams are readily available to those who may need assistance and to provide advice and assistance to farmers.”

He said farmers needed to consider new ways of producing crops and use the knowledge available to them.

“Maintaining food production is important for food security in the North.”

He said farmers, agriculture officers and communities needed to work together to ensure food continued to be produced despite the dry conditions.

item.title: Sala pitches cultural mentorship project
item.description: SALA Korosaya wants to build a village before a girl needs one. At this week’s FMF Hibiscus Festival private judging event, the Miss MHCC & Carpenters Towers contestant confronted troubling iTaukei statistics with a six-week cultural mentorship pilot.
item.content:encoded:
SALA Korosaya wants to build a village before a girl needs one.

At this week’s FMF Hibiscus Festival private judging event, the Miss MHCC & Carpenters Towers contestant confronted troubling iTaukei statistics with a six-week cultural mentorship pilot.

Three out of every four people in Fiji’s prisons are iTaukei.

About 90 per cent of new HIV diagnoses recorded in 2025 were among iTaukei people, while young people aged 15 to 29 accounted for about 60 per cent of new infections.

And of 1279 teenage pregnancies recorded between 2018 and 2021, 1,057 involved iTaukei girls, with the majority recorded in the Central Division.

For Sala, the statistics are uncomfortable – but avoiding them is worse.

“We are most imprisoned, most infected, most pregnant before we were ready,” the Miss MHCC & Carpenters Towers contestant said.

“That is my people, and I am not going to stand here and talk around it.”

She told the judges she intended to use the $5000 on a project she calls YAVU – a six-week cultural connection and mentorship program designed for 20 iTaukei young women aged 16 to 22.

She made it clear she was not presenting YAVU as a cure for Fiji’s social problems.

Instead, she is asking whether young women can be given stronger connections to culture, community and trusted adults before problems become crises.

She wants a young woman to know that before the statistics ever have a chance to define her, there is a village around her — and somewhere solid to stand.

Her idea came from an unexpected place: the pageant itself.

When Sala decided to enter, a group of people rallied around her — artisans, choreographers, coaches, designers, stylists and volunteers, including people who have worked with Hibiscus queens, national queens and Pacific queens.

What struck her was what happened after the pageants ended.

“The girls they prepared 10 years ago still call them. That team becomes a village around a young woman for the rest of her life.”

“Why does a girl only get that village if she enters a pageant?”

The name refers to the raised foundation of an ancestral house — the structure beneath the house that remains.

“The house can fall. YAVU stays, and it still tells you who you are.”

The program would use culture as the entry point rather than presenting participants with a conventional social intervention.

Over six weeks, the young women would learn meke, language, values and weaving while developing relationships with peers and older women.

Each participant would have a buddy, while every four girls would have a Matua – an older woman expected to remain connected to them beyond the program.

Sala is equally clear about the boundaries.

Professional referral pathways would therefore form part of the programme for participants requiring specialist support.

The cohort would also be deliberately mixed.

Ten places would be reserved for young women from higher-risk communities, while another 10 would be offered to girls from more settled homes who have never learned a meke.

She does not want to create a room full of young women labelled “at risk”.

“If I fill a room only with girls at risk, I have told every single one of them what I think she is. I will not do that.”

She wants the programme to build relationships across social and economic lines.

At the end of six weeks, the participants would complete an icoco, a large woven mat created collectively by the group.

item.title: Art beyond the prison walls
item.description: THE Fiji Corrections Service (FCS) launched its Yellow Ribbon Arts Exhibition, showcasing the creative works of inmates under the theme, “Behind the walls – expression of art, identity and renewal”. The exhibition was officially launched at the Grand Pacific Hotel on Thursday night, featuring artworks by seven inmate artists from the FCS Tagimoucia Art Gallery.
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Corrections Service (FCS) launched its Yellow Ribbon Arts Exhibition, showcasing the creative works of inmates under the theme, “Behind the walls – expression of art, identity and renewal”.

The exhibition was officially launched at the Grand Pacific Hotel on Thursday night, featuring artworks by seven inmate artists from the FCS Tagimoucia Art Gallery.

Among the featured artists was Aisake Qiolele, who was granted a presidential pardon last week after spending 21 years behind bars.

President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu, who officiated at the launch, highlighted the importance of rehabilitation and providing meaningful pathways for people transitioning back into society.

The event brought together government ministers, diplomatic representatives, members of the arts community, partners and supporters of the Yellow Ribbon initiative.

While the launch was by invitation only, members of the public will have an opportunity to view the remaining artworks at the Fiji Arts Council.
